Time-Dependent Perturbations and Selection Rules

What you need to know

  • A stationary state never changes. A perturbation that depends on time, such as the oscillating electric field of light, V^(t)=−M^Ecos⁡ωt\hat{V}(t) = -\hat{M}\mathcal{E}\cos\omega tV^(t)=−M^Ecosωt, makes the coefficients of the stationary states change: Ψ=∑ncn(t) e−iEnt/ℏψn\Psi = \sum_n c_n(t)\,e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\psi_nΨ=∑n​cn​(t)e−iEn​t/ℏψn​. A changing ∣cn∣2|c_n|^2∣cn​∣2 is a transition between levels.

  • To first order, a system that starts in state iii reaches state fff with the amplitude cf(t)=−(i/ℏ)∫0tVfi(t′) eiωfit′dt′c_f(t) = -(i/\hbar)\int_0^t V_{fi}(t')\,e^{i\omega_{fi}t'}dt'cf​(t)=−(i/ℏ)∫0t​Vfi​(t′)eiωfi​t′dt′, where Vfi=⟨f∣V^∣i⟩V_{fi} = \langle f|\hat{V}|i\rangleVfi​=⟨f∣V^∣i⟩ and ωfi=(Ef−Ei)/ℏ\omega_{fi} = (E_f - E_i)/\hbarωfi​=(Ef​−Ei​)/ℏ.

  • Resonance. The amplitude builds up only if the light stays in step with the Bohr frequency: ℏω=Ef−Ei\hbar\omega = E_f - E_iℏω=Ef​−Ei​. Bohr’s frequency condition is a result, and the line it gives has a width of about 1/t1/t1/t for light that acts for a time ttt.

  • Strength. The probability of the transition is proportional to the intensity of the light and to ∣⟨f∣M^∣i⟩∣2|\langle f|\hat{M}|i\rangle|^2∣⟨f∣M^∣i⟩∣2, the square of the transition dipole.

  • Selection rules. If the transition dipole is zero the transition is forbidden. Every selection rule of the course says when this one integral vanishes: Δv=±1\Delta v = \pm1Δv=±1, ΔJ=±1\Delta J = \pm1ΔJ=±1, Δl=±1\Delta l = \pm1Δl=±1.

What the earlier lectures left open¶

Spectroscopy has run through the course since Chapter 1, and three earlier lectures stopped just short of explaining it.

  • Lecture 3.7: a stationary state has a density that never moves. A superposition of two levels moves at the Bohr frequency ωfi=(Ef−Ei)/ℏ\omega_{fi} = (E_f - E_i)/\hbarωfi​=(Ef​−Ei​)/ℏ.

  • Lecture 4.3: a molecule in such a superposition has a swinging dipole, with amplitude ⟨f∣M^∣i⟩\langle f|\hat{M}|i\rangle⟨f∣M^∣i⟩. The lecture stated that the rate of absorption is proportional to the square of that integral, and promised the reason here.

  • Lectures 4.5 and 5.3: the same integral gave the selection rules of the rotor and of the hydrogen atom.

Three questions remain. How does light take a molecule out of a stationary state at all? Why only when hνh\nuhν matches a gap? And why is the rate set by ∣⟨f∣M^∣i⟩∣2|\langle f|\hat{M}|i\rangle|^2∣⟨f∣M^∣i⟩∣2?

Fig. The plan. Light adds a time-dependent term to the Hamiltonian, and the coefficients of the stationary states begin to change. Population reaches state fff only if the light is at resonance and the transition dipole is not zero. The rate is then proportional to the square of the transition dipole and to the intensity.

A Hamiltonian that changes in time¶

Light as a perturbation¶

A dipole MMM in an electric field E\mathcal{E}E has the energy −ME-M\mathcal{E}−ME (Lecture 4.3). In a light wave the field oscillates, so the molecule’s Hamiltonian gains a term that depends on time:

H^(t)=H^(0)+V^(t),V^(t)=−M^ Ecos⁡ωt\hat{H}(t) = \hat{H}^{(0)} + \hat{V}(t), \qquad \hat{V}(t) = -\hat{M}\,\mathcal{E}\cos\omega tH^(t)=H^(0)+V^(t),V^(t)=−M^Ecosωt
(1)

  • H^(0)\hat{H}^{(0)}H^(0) is the molecule alone, with known levels EnE_nEn​ and states ψn\psi_nψn​

  • E\mathcal{E}E is the amplitude of the field and ω=2πν\omega = 2\pi\nuω=2πν its angular frequency

  • M^\hat{M}M^ is the component of the dipole moment along the field: −ex-ex−ex for an electron, M(x)M(x)M(x) for a vibrating bond, Mecos⁡θM_e\cos\thetaMe​cosθ for a rotating molecule

  • The electric dipole approximation. Because the wavelength is so much longer than the molecule, the field is uniform over it, and its whole effect is the energy −ME(t)-M\mathcal{E}(t)−ME(t). The approximation is excellent from radio waves to the ultraviolet.

The coefficients move¶

Lecture 3.7 gave the recipe for time evolution when the Hamiltonian is fixed: expand in stationary states, and each term keeps its coefficient and turns its own phase,

Ψ(t)=∑ncn e−iEnt/ℏ ψn(cn constant)\Psi(t) = \sum_n c_n\,e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\,\psi_n \qquad (c_n\ \text{constant})Ψ(t)=n∑​cn​e−iEn​t/ℏψn​(cn​ constant)
(2)

With V^(t)\hat{V}(t)V^(t) switched on, the same expansion still works, since the ψn\psi_nψn​ are a complete set, but the coefficients now depend on time. ∣cn(t)∣2|c_n(t)|^2∣cn​(t)∣2 is the probability of finding the system in level nnn at time ttt. Three steps give their equation of motion.

  1. Insert the expansion into the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, iℏ ∂Ψ/∂t=(H^(0)+V^)Ψi\hbar\,\partial\Psi/\partial t = (\hat{H}^{(0)} + \hat{V})\Psiiℏ∂Ψ/∂t=(H^(0)+V^)Ψ. The time derivative acts on both cn(t)c_n(t)cn​(t) and the phase:

∑n(iℏ c˙n+Encn)e−iEnt/ℏ ψn=∑ncn(En+V^)e−iEnt/ℏ ψn\sum_n\left(i\hbar\,\dot{c}_n + E_nc_n\right)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\,\psi_n = \sum_n c_n\left(E_n + \hat{V}\right)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\,\psi_nn∑​(iℏc˙n​+En​cn​)e−iEn​t/ℏψn​=n∑​cn​(En​+V^)e−iEn​t/ℏψn​
(3)

  1. Cancel. The terms with EnE_nEn​ are the same on both sides: they are the evolution that happens anyway. What is left is driven by V^\hat{V}V^ alone:

∑niℏ c˙n e−iEnt/ℏ ψn=∑ncn e−iEnt/ℏ V^ψn\sum_n i\hbar\,\dot{c}_n\,e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\,\psi_n = \sum_n c_n\,e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\,\hat{V}\psi_nn∑​iℏc˙n​e−iEn​t/ℏψn​=n∑​cn​e−iEn​t/ℏV^ψn​
(4)

  1. Project onto one state. Multiply by ψm∗\psi_m^*ψm∗​ and integrate. Orthonormality leaves a single term on the left:

iℏ dcmdt=∑nVmn(t) eiωmnt cni\hbar\,\frac{dc_m}{dt} = \sum_n V_{mn}(t)\,e^{i\omega_{mn}t}\,c_niℏdtdcm​​=n∑​Vmn​(t)eiωmn​tcn​
(5)

with Vmn(t)=⟨m∣V^(t)∣n⟩V_{mn}(t) = \langle m|\hat{V}(t)|n\rangleVmn​(t)=⟨m∣V^(t)∣n⟩ and ωmn=(Em−En)/ℏ\omega_{mn} = (E_m - E_n)/\hbarωmn​=(Em​−En​)/ℏ.

  • Nothing has been approximated yet. With V^=0\hat{V} = 0V^=0 every cmc_mcm​ is constant, which is Lecture 3.7.

  • A matrix element opens each channel. Population flows from state nnn to state mmm only through VmnV_{mn}Vmn​, the matrix element of the perturbation between them, the same kind of integral that Lecture 6.2 used.

  • Each channel carries a Bohr frequency. The factor eiωmnte^{i\omega_{mn}t}eiωmn​t is the difference between the phases of the two stationary states.

First order: a weak perturbation¶

Let the system start in one stationary state, iii: ci(0)=1c_i(0) = 1ci​(0)=1 and every other coefficient zero. If the perturbation is weak, the coefficients change slowly, and on the right-hand side they can be replaced by their starting values. Only the term n=in = in=i survives:

iℏ dcfdt=Vfi(t) eiωfiti\hbar\,\frac{dc_f}{dt} = V_{fi}(t)\,e^{i\omega_{fi}t}iℏdtdcf​​=Vfi​(t)eiωfi​t
(6)

Integrating from the moment the perturbation is switched on:

First-order transition amplitude
cf(t)=−iℏ∫0tVfi(t′) eiωfit′ dt′,Pi→f(t)=∣cf(t)∣2c_f(t) = -\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^t V_{fi}(t')\,e^{i\omega_{fi}t'}\,dt', \qquad P_{i \to f}(t) = |c_f(t)|^2cf​(t)=−ℏi​∫0t​Vfi​(t′)eiωfi​t′dt′,Pi→f​(t)=∣cf​(t)∣2
(7)

  • iii is the initial state and fff the final one; Vfi=⟨f∣V^∣i⟩V_{fi} = \langle f|\hat{V}|i\rangleVfi​=⟨f∣V^∣i⟩ and ωfi=(Ef−Ei)/ℏ\omega_{fi} = (E_f - E_i)/\hbarωfi​=(Ef​−Ei​)/ℏ

  • Valid while Pi→fP_{i \to f}Pi→f​ stays small

  • Two conditions are already visible. The matrix element VfiV_{fi}Vfi​ must not vanish, and the integral must not average to zero.

  • The integral is a sum of pushes. eiωfit′e^{i\omega_{fi}t'}eiωfi​t′ turns steadily, like a child on a swing. If Vfi(t′)V_{fi}(t')Vfi​(t′) is constant, the pushes point in every direction in turn and cancel. They add up only if Vfi(t′)V_{fi}(t')Vfi​(t′) itself oscillates at the frequency ωfi\omega_{fi}ωfi​.

Light at frequency ω\omegaω: resonance¶

The integral¶

For light, Vfi(t)=−Mfi Ecos⁡ωtV_{fi}(t) = -M_{fi}\,\mathcal{E}\cos\omega tVfi​(t)=−Mfi​Ecosωt, where Mfi=⟨f∣M^∣i⟩M_{fi} = \langle f|\hat{M}|i\rangleMfi​=⟨f∣M^∣i⟩ is the transition dipole. Write the cosine as two exponentials, cos⁡ωt=12(eiωt+e−iωt)\cos\omega t = \frac{1}{2}(e^{i\omega t} + e^{-i\omega t})cosωt=21​(eiωt+e−iωt):

cf(t)=iMfi E2ℏ∫0t[ei(ωfi+ω)t′+ei(ωfi−ω)t′]dt′c_f(t) = \frac{iM_{fi}\,\mathcal{E}}{2\hbar}\int_0^t\left[e^{i(\omega_{fi} + \omega)t'} + e^{i(\omega_{fi} - \omega)t'}\right]dt'cf​(t)=2ℏiMfi​E​∫0t​[ei(ωfi​+ω)t′+ei(ωfi​−ω)t′]dt′
(8)

Take absorption, Ef>EiE_f > E_iEf​>Ei​, with the light tuned near the gap, ω≈ωfi\omega \approx \omega_{fi}ω≈ωfi​. The first exponential turns at about 2ω2\omega2ω, some 1015 times a second for visible light, and its integral never grows. The second turns at the slow rate

δ=ωfi−ω\delta = \omega_{fi} - \omegaδ=ωfi​−ω
(9)

the detuning of the light from the transition. Keeping that term, ∫0teiδt′dt′=(eiδt−1)/iδ\int_0^t e^{i\delta t'}dt' = (e^{i\delta t} - 1)/i\delta∫0t​eiδt′dt′=(eiδt−1)/iδ, and with ∣eiδt−1∣2=4sin⁡2(δt/2)|e^{i\delta t} - 1|^2 = 4\sin^2(\delta t/2)∣eiδt−1∣2=4sin2(δt/2):

Absorption of light, to first order
Pi→f(t)=∣Mfi∣2 E2ℏ2  sin⁡2 ⁣[(ωfi−ω) t/2](ωfi−ω)2,Mfi=⟨f∣M^∣i⟩P_{i \to f}(t) = \frac{|M_{fi}|^2\,\mathcal{E}^2}{\hbar^2}\;\frac{\sin^2\!\left[(\omega_{fi} - \omega)\,t/2\right]}{(\omega_{fi} - \omega)^2}, \qquad M_{fi} = \langle f|\hat{M}|i\ranglePi→f​(t)=ℏ2∣Mfi​∣2E2​(ωfi​−ω)2sin2[(ωfi​−ω)t/2]​,Mfi​=⟨f∣M^∣i⟩
(10)

  • E\mathcal{E}E and ω\omegaω are the amplitude and frequency of the light, on for a time ttt

  • On resonance, ω=ωfi\omega = \omega_{fi}ω=ωfi​, it becomes Pi→f=(∣Mfi∣ E t/2ℏ)2P_{i \to f} = \left(|M_{fi}|\,\mathcal{E}\,t/2\hbar\right)^2Pi→f​=(∣Mfi​∣Et/2ℏ)2

Fig. The first-order probability of reaching state fff. Left: against time. On resonance it grows as t2t^2t2; off resonance it rises, falls back to zero and never builds up. Right: against the frequency of the light, after a time ttt and after 2t2t2t. The peak at ωfi\omega_{fi}ωfi​ becomes four times taller and half as wide.

Reading the result¶

  • Bohr’s frequency condition, derived. The transition happens when ℏω=Ef−Ei\hbar\omega = E_f - E_iℏω=Ef​−Ei​. Lecture 1.5 took this as a postulate and Lecture 3.7 saw it in the motion of a superposition. Here it is the condition for the pushes of the light to stay in step with the system.

  • The line has a width. The peak reaches zero at ωfi±2π/t\omega_{fi} \pm 2\pi/tωfi​±2π/t. Light that acts for a time ttt does not have a frequency defined better than about 1/t1/t1/t: δν⋅t≈1\delta\nu\cdot t \approx 1δν⋅t≈1. A laser pulse 10 fs long is some 3000 cm−1^{-1}−1 wide, covers many vibrational levels at once, and launches the vibrating wave packets of Lecture 3.7.

  • Strength. The probability is proportional to E2\mathcal{E}^2E2, which is the intensity of the light, and to ∣Mfi∣2|M_{fi}|^2∣Mfi​∣2, the square of the transition dipole. This is the statement Lecture 4.3 borrowed.

  • Emission is the same process run backward. If the system starts in the upper level, the other exponential is the resonant one and the result is identical. Light at resonance drives a molecule down as readily as up: stimulated emission, the process a laser runs on.

  • Ordinary light gives a steady rate. No light source has a single frequency. Added over a band of frequencies, the peak of the figure contributes its area, which grows in proportion to ttt: the height goes as t2t^2t2 and the width as 1/t1/t1/t. A probability proportional to time is a constant rate of absorption, proportional to ∣Mfi∣2|M_{fi}|^2∣Mfi​∣2 and to the intensity of the light at ωfi\omega_{fi}ωfi​. Summed over the molecules in a beam’s path, this is the Beer-Lambert law.

Going further: the rate of absorption (Fermi’s golden rule)

For light arriving from all directions with an energy density u(ω)u(\omega)u(ω) per unit of angular frequency, the rate is

Wi→f=π3ε0ℏ2 ∣Mfi∣2 u(ωfi)W_{i \to f} = \frac{\pi}{3\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}\,|M_{fi}|^2\,u(\omega_{fi})Wi→f​=3ε0​ℏ2π​∣Mfi​∣2u(ωfi​)
(11)

a form of Fermi’s golden rule: rate === (coupling)2^22 ×\times× (how much there is to couple to). Three steps lead from the first-order probability, written as P=(∣Mfi∣2E2/4ℏ2) sin⁡2(δt/2)/(δ/2)2P = (|M_{fi}|^2\mathcal{E}^2/4\hbar^2)\,\sin^2(\delta t/2)/(\delta/2)^2P=(∣Mfi​∣2E2/4ℏ2)sin2(δt/2)/(δ/2)2, to this rate.

  1. A wave of amplitude E\mathcal{E}E has the energy density 12ε0E2\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0\mathcal{E}^221​ε0​E2. For a band of frequencies replace E2\mathcal{E}^2E2 by 2u(ω) dω/ε02u(\omega)\,d\omega/\varepsilon_02u(ω)dω/ε0​ and integrate over ω\omegaω.

  2. The peak is narrow, so u(ω)u(\omega)u(ω) can be taken at ωfi\omega_{fi}ωfi​ and moved outside. What remains is ∫sin⁡2(δt/2)/(δ/2)2 dδ=2πt\int\sin^2(\delta t/2)/(\delta/2)^2\,d\delta = 2\pi t∫sin2(δt/2)/(δ/2)2dδ=2πt.

  3. The field points in a random direction relative to the dipole. The average of cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 of the angle between them, over all directions, is 13\frac{1}{3}31​.

P=∣Mfi∣24ℏ2⋅2u(ωfi)ε0⋅2πt⋅13=π∣Mfi∣2 u(ωfi)3ε0ℏ2  tP = \frac{|M_{fi}|^2}{4\hbar^2}\cdot\frac{2u(\omega_{fi})}{\varepsilon_0}\cdot2\pi t\cdot\frac{1}{3} = \frac{\pi|M_{fi}|^2\,u(\omega_{fi})}{3\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}\;tP=4ℏ2∣Mfi​∣2​⋅ε0​2u(ωfi​)​⋅2πt⋅31​=3ε0​ℏ2π∣Mfi​∣2u(ωfi​)​t
(12)

Here ∣Mfi∣2|M_{fi}|^2∣Mfi​∣2 is the sum of the squares of the three components of the transition dipole. The same rate applies downward, for stimulated emission.

Watching a transition¶

First order holds only while the probability is small. Followed all the way, light exactly at resonance moves the whole population to the upper level. The figure follows that process for a particle in a box, driven from ψ1\psi_1ψ1​ to ψ2\psi_2ψ2​:

Source
# synced: drive_two_level
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
p1, p2 = np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(np.pi * x), np.sqrt(2) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
frames, swings = 36, 4                                           # one pi pulse; the dipole swings four times during it
s = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)                                       # time in units of the pulse length pi / Omega
x12 = -16 / (9 * np.pi**2)
dip = lambda u: x12 * np.sin(np.pi * u) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * swings * u)   # <x> - L/2 during the pulse
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8.6, 4.0))
ax = fig.add_axes([0.05, 0.13, 0.4, 0.8])
bx = fig.add_axes([0.58, 0.6, 0.39, 0.33]); cx = fig.add_axes([0.58, 0.13, 0.39, 0.33])
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, 4.2], color="k", lw=2.4); ax.plot([1, 1], [0, 4.2], color="k", lw=2.4); ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 0], color="k", lw=2.4)
line, = ax.plot(x, p1**2, color=TEAL, lw=2.4)
fill = [ax.fill_between(x, 0, p1**2, color=TEAL, alpha=0.3, lw=0)]
ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 1.05); ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 4.2); ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0", "$L$"]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False); ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False); ax.tick_params(labelsize=12, length=0)
ax.set_ylabel(r"$|\Psi(x, t)|^2$", fontsize=13)
bx.plot(s, np.cos(np.pi * s / 2) ** 2, color=TEAL, lw=2.2); bx.plot(s, np.sin(np.pi * s / 2) ** 2, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2)
bx.text(0.03, 0.8, r"$|c_1|^2$", color=TEAL, fontsize=12.5, va="center"); bx.text(0.97, 0.8, r"$|c_2|^2$", color=ORANGE, fontsize=12.5, va="center", ha="right")
d1, = bx.plot([0], [1], "o", color=TEAL, ms=8, clip_on=False); d2, = bx.plot([0], [0], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=8, clip_on=False)
bx.set_xlim(0, 1); bx.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.08); bx.set_xticks([]); bx.set_yticks([0, 1]); bx.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
cx.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)
cx.plot(s, dip(s), color="#ced4da", lw=1.4)
trace, = cx.plot([], [], color="k", lw=2.0)
d3, = cx.plot([0], [0], "o", color="k", ms=7, clip_on=False)
cx.set_xlim(0, 1); cx.set_ylim(-0.22, 0.22); cx.set_xticks([0, 1]); cx.set_xticklabels(["0", r"$\pi/\Omega$"]); cx.set_yticks([])
cx.spines["left"].set_visible(False); cx.tick_params(labelsize=12)
cx.set_xlabel("time", fontsize=12.5); cx.set_ylabel(r"$\langle x\rangle - L/2$", fontsize=12.5)

def update(k):
    u = k / (frames - 1)
    c1, c2 = np.cos(np.pi * u / 2), np.sin(np.pi * u / 2)
    rho = c1**2 * p1**2 + c2**2 * p2**2 + 2 * c1 * c2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * swings * u) * p1 * p2
    line.set_ydata(rho)
    fill[0].remove()
    fill[0] = ax.fill_between(x, 0, rho, color=TEAL, alpha=0.3, lw=0)
    d1.set_data([u], [c1**2]); d2.set_data([u], [c2**2])
    m = s <= u
    trace.set_data(s[m], dip(s[m])); d3.set_data([u], [dip(u)])

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=110, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

Fig. Light at resonance acting on a particle in a box. Left: the density, which starts as ∣ψ1∣2|\psi_1|^2∣ψ1​∣2 and ends as ∣ψ2∣2|\psi_2|^2∣ψ2​∣2. Right, top: the two populations. Right, bottom: the average position, which is the dipole. Press play.

  • In between, the density sloshes. The state is a superposition of ψ1\psi_1ψ1​ and ψ2\psi_2ψ2​, and its density swings from side to side at the Bohr frequency, as in Lecture 3.2.

  • The dipole swings only during the transition. ⟨x⟩\langle x\rangle⟨x⟩ is still at the start and at the end, when the system is in one stationary state, and swings most at the midpoint, when the populations are equal. A molecule exchanges energy with light through this swinging dipole, as Lecture 4.3 said.

Drive the two levels yourself. On resonance the population goes all the way up and comes back; move the detuning away from zero and the transfer collapses. The dashed curve is first order, good only at the start.

Going further: strong light and Rabi oscillations

For two levels the equations of motion can be solved without assuming that the coefficients stay near their starting values. Keeping the resonant term, they read

dcfdt=iΩ2 eiδt ci,dcidt=iΩ2 e−iδt cf\frac{dc_f}{dt} = \frac{i\Omega}{2}\,e^{i\delta t}\,c_i, \qquad \frac{dc_i}{dt} = \frac{i\Omega}{2}\,e^{-i\delta t}\,c_fdtdcf​​=2iΩ​eiδtci​,dtdci​​=2iΩ​e−iδtcf​
(13)
Ω=∣Mfi∣ Eℏ\Omega = \frac{|M_{fi}|\,\mathcal{E}}{\hbar}Ω=ℏ∣Mfi​∣E​
(14)

Ω\OmegaΩ is the Rabi frequency: the transition dipole times the field, in units of ℏ\hbarℏ. On resonance (δ=0\delta = 0δ=0), differentiating the first equation and inserting the second gives c¨f=−(Ω/2)2cf\ddot{c}_f = -(\Omega/2)^2c_fc¨f​=−(Ω/2)2cf​, the equation of a harmonic oscillator, so cf=isin⁡(Ωt/2)c_f = i\sin(\Omega t/2)cf​=isin(Ωt/2) and ci=cos⁡(Ωt/2)c_i = \cos(\Omega t/2)ci​=cos(Ωt/2). In general,

Pi→f(t)=Ω2Ω2+δ2 sin⁡2 ⁣(12Ω2+δ2  t)P_{i \to f}(t) = \frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2 + \delta^2}\,\sin^2\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\Omega^2 + \delta^2}\;t\right)Pi→f​(t)=Ω2+δ2Ω2​sin2(21​Ω2+δ2​t)
(15)

  • This is the two-level problem of Lecture 6.1 once more, with the coupling 12ℏΩ\frac{1}{2}\hbar\Omega21​ℏΩ and the gap ℏδ\hbar\deltaℏδ: the square root Ω2+δ2\sqrt{\Omega^2 + \delta^2}Ω2+δ2​ is the same one that gave E±E_\pmE±​.

  • A π\piπ pulse inverts the population. Light at resonance, left on for t=π/Ωt = \pi/\Omegat=π/Ω, moves every molecule from iii to fff. Left on longer, it brings them back down by stimulated emission.

  • A π/2\pi/2π/2 pulse makes the equal superposition, the state whose dipole swings with the largest amplitude. NMR works with exactly these pulses, applied to the two spin levels of Lecture 5.3 with the magnetic field of a radio wave in place of E\mathcal{E}E (Problem 3).

  • For short times sin⁡2x≈x2\sin^2x \approx x^2sin2x≈x2 returns the first-order result.

  • Why an ordinary spectrometer shows no oscillation. Its light is weak and has many frequencies, and collisions interrupt each molecule long before Ωt\Omega tΩt reaches 1. Every molecule stays in the first-order regime, and the result is a steady rate.

Selection rules¶

Allowed and forbidden¶

Every result of this lecture carries the factor ∣Mfi∣2|M_{fi}|^2∣Mfi​∣2. If the transition dipole is zero, light of any intensity and any frequency leaves the transition untouched.

The selection rule for electric dipole transitions
allowed only ifMfi=⟨f∣M^∣i⟩=∫ψf∗ M^ ψi dτ  ≠  0\text{allowed only if}\qquad M_{fi} = \langle f|\hat{M}|i\rangle = \int\psi_f^*\,\hat{M}\,\psi_i\,d\tau \;\neq\; 0allowed only ifMfi​=⟨f∣M^∣i⟩=∫ψf∗​M^ψi​dτ=0
(16)

  • The integral depends on the two states and on the dipole operator, not on the light

  • A rule on quantum numbers (such as Δv=±1\Delta v = \pm1Δv=±1) is a statement of when this integral vanishes

Source

Two general arguments settle most cases without an integral.

  • Parity. The dipole operator is odd: it changes sign when every coordinate does. The integrand ψf∗M^ψi\psi_f^*\hat{M}\psi_iψf∗​M^ψi​ is then odd, and the integral zero, unless the two states have opposite parity. This is the sandwich rule of Lecture 4.2, and in atoms it is called the Laporte rule: s to p and p to d are allowed, s to s and d to d are not.

  • Angular momentum. A photon carries one unit of angular momentum, ℏ\hbarℏ. Absorbing or emitting one changes the angular momentum of the molecule by one unit: ΔJ=±1\Delta J = \pm1ΔJ=±1, Δl=±1\Delta l = \pm1Δl=±1.

Example: an electron in a box

For an electron in a box of length LLL, find the transition dipoles from n=1n = 1n=1 to n=2n = 2n=2 and to n=3n = 3n=3.

With M^=−ex\hat{M} = -exM^=−ex and the matrix elements of Lecture 3.7,

M21=−e ⟨2∣x∣1⟩=169π2 eL=0.18 eLM_{21} = -e\,\langle 2|x|1\rangle = \frac{16}{9\pi^2}\,eL = 0.18\,eLM21​=−e⟨2∣x∣1⟩=9π216​eL=0.18eL
(17)
M31=−e ⟨3∣x∣1⟩=0M_{31} = -e\,\langle 3|x|1\rangle = 0M31​=−e⟨3∣x∣1⟩=0
(18)

1→21 \to 21→2 is allowed: the two states have opposite parity about the middle of the box. 1→31 \to 31→3 is forbidden: both are even, x−L/2x - L/2x−L/2 is odd, and the integrand is odd. For L=1L = 1L=1 nm, M21=8.7M_{21} = 8.7M21​=8.7 D, a large transition dipole, which is why conjugated dyes absorb so strongly.

Forbidden does not mean never¶

A forbidden transition has a zero electric dipole matrix element. Weaker mechanisms remain: the magnetic field of the light, the variation of the field across the molecule, two photons at once, or a small mixing of states that breaks the rule. They show up as lines thousands or millions of times weaker, and as excited states that take a long time to emit their photon:

excited statewhy it decays slowly or fastlifetime
H 2pallowed, Δl=−1\Delta l = -1Δl=−11.6 ns
H 2sΔl=0\Delta l = 0Δl=0: forbidden, decays by two photons0.12 s
triplet state of an organic dye (phosphorescence)ΔS≠0\Delta S \neq 0ΔS=0: the field does not act on spinms to s
upper hyperfine level of H (the 21 cm line)magnetic dipole, and a very low frequency107 years
Going further: spontaneous emission, lifetimes and linewidths

Stimulated emission needs light already present. An excited atom in complete darkness still emits: spontaneous emission. The oscillating field of this lecture is a classical wave and cannot explain it; that takes the quantum theory of the electromagnetic field itself. Einstein found the rate in 1917 by requiring absorption, stimulated emission and spontaneous emission to keep matter and blackbody radiation in equilibrium:

Af→i=ωfi3 ∣Mfi∣23πε0ℏc3,τ=1AA_{f \to i} = \frac{\omega_{fi}^3\,|M_{fi}|^2}{3\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar c^3}, \qquad \tau = \frac{1}{A}Af→i​=3πε0​ℏc3ωfi3​∣Mfi​∣2​,τ=A1​
(19)

AAA is the probability per unit time that the excited state emits a photon, and τ\tauτ is its lifetime.

  • The same transition dipole as absorption, so a forbidden line is weak in absorption and slow in emission.

  • The ω3\omega^3ω3 decides where spontaneous emission matters. In the ultraviolet and visible it empties excited states in nanoseconds. In the infrared it takes milliseconds, and collisions usually win. At radio frequencies it takes years: the spins of an NMR experiment never relax by emitting photons.

  • Hydrogen’s 2p state. With Ef−Ei=10.2E_f - E_i = 10.2Ef​−Ei​=10.2 eV, so ωfi=1.55×1016\omega_{fi} = 1.55\times10^{16}ωfi​=1.55×1016 s−1^{-1}−1, and ∣Mfi∣=0.745 ea0=6.32×10−30|M_{fi}| = 0.745\,ea_0 = 6.32\times10^{-30}∣Mfi​∣=0.745ea0​=6.32×10−30 C m (Problem 5), the formula gives A=6.3×108A = 6.3\times10^8A=6.3×108 s−1^{-1}−1 and τ=1.6\tau = 1.6τ=1.6 ns, the measured lifetime.

  • Natural linewidth. A state that lasts a time τ\tauτ emits a wave train about that long, and a wave of limited duration has a spread of frequencies, as in the resonance section: δν=1/2πτ\delta\nu = 1/2\pi\tauδν=1/2πτ. For the 2p state of hydrogen that is 100 MHz.

  • Anything that shortens the life broadens the line. Collisions in a gas or a liquid interrupt the excited state and add to the width, which is one reason spectra of liquids are broad and spectra of dilute gases sharp.

With these three tools the course leaves the systems that can be solved exactly. Chapter 7 applies the first two to atoms with more than one electron, and Chapter 8 to molecules.

Problems¶

Problem 1: A perturbation that is switched on and left on¶

A constant perturbation V^\hat{V}V^ is switched on at t=0t = 0t=0 and left on. (a) Use the first-order amplitude to find the probability of state fff at time ttt. (b) What is its largest value, and its average over time? (c) Compare with the first-order mixing coefficient of Lecture 6.2. Does a constant perturbation cause lasting transitions?

Solution

(a) With VfiV_{fi}Vfi​ constant,

cf(t)=−iVfiℏ∫0teiωfit′dt′=−Vfiℏωfi(eiωfit−1)c_f(t) = -\frac{iV_{fi}}{\hbar}\int_0^t e^{i\omega_{fi}t'}dt' = -\frac{V_{fi}}{\hbar\omega_{fi}}\left(e^{i\omega_{fi}t} - 1\right)cf​(t)=−ℏiVfi​​∫0t​eiωfi​t′dt′=−ℏωfi​Vfi​​(eiωfi​t−1)
(20)
Pi→f(t)=4∣Vfi∣2(Ef−Ei)2 sin⁡2ωfit2P_{i \to f}(t) = \frac{4|V_{fi}|^2}{(E_f - E_i)^2}\,\sin^2\frac{\omega_{fi}t}{2}Pi→f​(t)=(Ef​−Ei​)24∣Vfi​∣2​sin22ωfi​t​
(21)

(b) The probability oscillates between zero and 4∣Vfi∣2/(Ef−Ei)24|V_{fi}|^2/(E_f - E_i)^24∣Vfi​∣2/(Ef​−Ei​)2, with the average 2∣Vfi∣2/(Ef−Ei)22|V_{fi}|^2/(E_f - E_i)^22∣Vfi​∣2/(Ef​−Ei​)2. It never grows.

(c) Lecture 6.2 found that a constant perturbation changes state iii into ψi(0)+∑kckψk(0)\psi_i^{(0)} + \sum_k c_k\psi_k^{(0)}ψi(0)​+∑k​ck​ψk(0)​ with ∣cf∣2=∣Vfi∣2/(Ef−Ei)2|c_f|^2 = |V_{fi}|^2/(E_f - E_i)^2∣cf​∣2=∣Vfi​∣2/(Ef​−Ei​)2: the same combination of coupling over gap. The system has not made a transition; it has been pushed from an eigenstate of the old Hamiltonian into a mixture of eigenstates of the new one, and the oscillation is that mixture beating. The amplitude is twice the static value because the perturbation was switched on suddenly. A lasting, growing transfer needs a perturbation that oscillates at ωfi\omega_{fi}ωfi​.

Problem 2: How short a pulse makes a wave packet?¶

A laser pulse lasts 10 fs. (a) Estimate the spread of its frequencies from δν≈1/t\delta\nu \approx 1/tδν≈1/t, in Hz and in cm−1^{-1}−1. (b) The vibrational levels of I2_22​ in its excited state are about 100 cm−1^{-1}−1 apart, and those of HCl are 2886 cm−1^{-1}−1 apart. For which molecule does the pulse cover several levels at once? (c) What does the molecule do after such a pulse? Connect your answer to the Morse packet of Lecture 3.7. (d) How long must a pulse be to excite a single vibrational level of I2_22​?

Problem 3: A 90° pulse in NMR¶

This problem uses the Going further box on Rabi oscillations. In NMR the two levels are the spin states of a proton in a field B0B_0B0​, and the perturbation is a magnetic field B1B_1B1​ rotating at the radio frequency. Its Rabi frequency is Ω=γB1\Omega = \gamma B_1Ω=γB1​, with γ=2.675×108\gamma = 2.675\times10^8γ=2.675×108 rad s−1^{-1}−1 T−1^{-1}−1 for the proton. (a) What B1B_1B1​ gives a π/2\pi/2π/2 pulse in 10 μs? (b) The pulse lasts 10 μs. How wide a band of frequencies does it excite? Compare with the range of proton resonances in a 400 MHz spectrometer, about 10 ppm.

Solution

(a) A π/2\pi/2π/2 pulse has Ωt=π/2\Omega t = \pi/2Ωt=π/2:

B1=π/2γt=1.571(2.675×108)(1.0×10−5) T=5.9×10−4 TB_1 = \frac{\pi/2}{\gamma t} = \frac{1.571}{(2.675\times10^8)(1.0\times10^{-5})}\ \text{T} = 5.9\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}B1​=γtπ/2​=(2.675×108)(1.0×10−5)1.571​ T=5.9×10−4 T
(22)

about 0.6 mT, some 16 000 times weaker than the 9.4 T field B0B_0B0​ that sets the resonance frequency. It works because it is at resonance.

(b) A pulse of length ttt has a width of about 1/t=1051/t = 10^51/t=105 Hz. Ten parts per million of 400 MHz is 4000 Hz. The pulse is 25 times broader than the whole spectrum, so it excites every proton in the sample equally, whatever its chemical shift. After the pulse each spin is in an equal superposition and its magnetic moment swings at its own frequency; the spectrometer records the sum of all those oscillations and separates the frequencies by a Fourier transform (Appendix A.6). This is why a modern NMR experiment takes seconds and not the hours needed to sweep the frequency slowly.

Problem 4: Allowed or forbidden?¶

Decide whether each transition is allowed for electric dipole radiation, and name the rule you used: (a) a particle in a box, n=2→4n = 2 \to 4n=2→4; (b) the same, n=2→3n = 2 \to 3n=2→3; (c) a harmonic oscillator, v=0→2v = 0 \to 2v=0→2; (d) HCl, J=1→2J = 1 \to 2J=1→2; (e) N2_22​, J=1→2J = 1 \to 2J=1→2; (f) hydrogen, 3d→2p3\text{d} \to 2\text{p}3d→2p; (g) hydrogen, 3d→1s3\text{d} \to 1\text{s}3d→1s; (h) hydrogen, 3s→1s3\text{s} \to 1\text{s}3s→1s; (i) a triplet state of a molecule to its singlet ground state.

Problem 5: The transition dipole of Lyman α¶

Compute the transition dipole ⟨2pz∣−ez∣1s⟩\langle 2\text{p}_z|{-ez}|1\text{s}\rangle⟨2pz​∣−ez∣1s⟩ of hydrogen, using z=rcos⁡θz = r\cos\thetaz=rcosθ, R10=2e−rR_{10} = 2e^{-r}R10​=2e−r, R21=re−r/2/26R_{21} = re^{-r/2}/2\sqrt{6}R21​=re−r/2/26​ (atomic units), Y00=1/4πY_0^0 = 1/\sqrt{4\pi}Y00​=1/4π​ and Y10=3/4πcos⁡θY_1^0 = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\cos\thetaY10​=3/4π​cosθ. Then show that ⟨2s∣z∣1s⟩=0\langle 2\text{s}|z|1\text{s}\rangle = 0⟨2s∣z∣1s⟩=0.

⟨2pz∣z∣1s⟩=∫0∞R21 r R10 r2 dr  ×∫Y10cos⁡θ  Y00 dΩ\langle 2\text{p}_z|z|1\text{s}\rangle = \int_0^\infty R_{21}\,r\,R_{10}\,r^2\,dr\;\times\int Y_1^0\cos\theta\;Y_0^0\,d\Omega⟨2pz​∣z∣1s⟩=∫0∞​R21​rR10​r2dr×∫Y10​cosθY00​dΩ
(23)

Radial part, with ∫0∞rne−ardr=n!/an+1\int_0^\infty r^ne^{-ar}dr = n!/a^{n+1}∫0∞​rne−ardr=n!/an+1:

16∫0∞r4e−3r/2 dr=16⋅4!(3/2)5=7682436=1.290 a0\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\int_0^\infty r^4e^{-3r/2}\,dr = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot\frac{4!}{(3/2)^5} = \frac{768}{243\sqrt{6}} = 1.290\ a_06​1​∫0∞​r4e−3r/2dr=6​1​⋅(3/2)54!​=2436​768​=1.290 a0​
(24)

Angular part: cos⁡θ Y00=Y10/3\cos\theta\,Y_0^0 = Y_1^0/\sqrt{3}cosθY00​=Y10​/3​, so the integral is 13∫∣Y10∣2dΩ=1/3\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int|Y_1^0|^2d\Omega = 1/\sqrt{3}3​1​∫∣Y10​∣2dΩ=1/3​. Together,

⟨2pz∣z∣1s⟩=1.2903 a0=1282243 a0=0.745 a0\langle 2\text{p}_z|z|1\text{s}\rangle = \frac{1.290}{\sqrt{3}}\,a_0 = \frac{128\sqrt{2}}{243}\,a_0 = 0.745\,a_0⟨2pz​∣z∣1s⟩=3​1.290​a0​=2431282​​a0​=0.745a0​
(25)

For 2s→1s2\text{s} \to 1\text{s}2s→1s the angular part is ∫Y00cos⁡θ Y00 dΩ=14π∫cos⁡θ dΩ=0\int Y_0^0\cos\theta\,Y_0^0\,d\Omega = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int\cos\theta\,d\Omega = 0∫Y00​cosθY00​dΩ=4π1​∫cosθdΩ=0: the average of cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ over a sphere vanishes. Whatever the radial integral, the transition dipole is zero. This is Δl=0\Delta l = 0Δl=0, forbidden, and the reason the 2s state is metastable.

Problem 6: The sodium D line¶

This problem uses the Going further box on spontaneous emission. The 3p state of sodium lives 16.2 ns and decays to 3s by emitting the yellow D line at 589 nm. (a) Find the natural width of the line in MHz. The two D lines are 17.2 cm−1^{-1}−1 apart (Lecture 5.3): is the doublet resolved in spite of the natural width? (b) Invert the formula for AAA to find the transition dipole, in units of ea0ea_0ea0​ and in debye. Is your answer a reasonable size for an atom? (c) The 3p state of sodium and the 2p state of hydrogen are both allowed. Why does sodium’s live ten times longer?

Problem 7: Why steady light cannot empty the lower level¶

NiN_iNi​ molecules are in the lower of two levels and NfN_fNf​ in the upper. Light at resonance drives both absorption and stimulated emission at the same rate WWW per molecule. Ignore spontaneous emission. (a) Write dNf/dtdN_f/dtdNf​/dt. (b) What is the net rate at which energy is absorbed from the light? (c) What happens to the populations if the light is left on, and what happens to the absorption? (d) Apply your answer to NMR, where Lecture 5.3 found a population difference of 32 per million.

Solution

(a) Each lower molecule goes up at the rate WWW and each upper one comes down at the same rate:

dNfdt=WNi−WNf=W (Ni−Nf)\frac{dN_f}{dt} = W N_i - W N_f = W\,(N_i - N_f)dtdNf​​=WNi​−WNf​=W(Ni​−Nf​)
(27)

(b) Each upward step removes a photon of energy ℏω\hbar\omegaℏω and each downward step adds one, so the net power absorbed is ℏω W (Ni−Nf)\hbar\omega\,W\,(N_i - N_f)ℏωW(Ni​−Nf​). Absorption is proportional to the difference of the populations, not to the number of molecules.

(c) With N=Ni+NfN = N_i + N_fN=Ni​+Nf​ fixed, Ni−NfN_i - N_fNi​−Nf​ obeys d(Ni−Nf)/dt=−2W(Ni−Nf)d(N_i - N_f)/dt = -2W(N_i - N_f)d(Ni​−Nf​)/dt=−2W(Ni​−Nf​) and decays to zero. The populations become equal, and the net absorption stops: the transition is saturated. Steady light can never put more molecules in the upper level than in the lower. A laser, which needs more molecules up than down, must reach its upper level by a detour through a third level.

(d) In NMR the two levels are so close that at room temperature only 32 spins per million more are in the lower one. The signal comes from that small excess alone, which is why NMR is an insensitive method and why stronger magnets, which widen the gap and the population difference, are worth their cost. Too much radio-frequency power saturates the transition and the signal disappears.

Problem 8: Exact against first order¶

This problem uses the Going further box on Rabi oscillations. (a) Show that for short times the exact two-level probability reduces to the first-order result, both on resonance and off. (b) On resonance, at what value of Ωt\Omega tΩt is first order 10% too high? (c) How far must the light be detuned, in units of Ω\OmegaΩ, for the largest transfer to be 50%? 10%? Check both with the widget. (d) Doubling the field strength doubles Ω\OmegaΩ. At a fixed detuning, what does that do to the largest transfer, and to the range of frequencies over which a transition responds?
